title: Ultra-low energy (20 - 300 eV) electron imaging and diffraction
abstract: The lecture discusses the properties of low-energy electrons compared to the electrons of conventional energies employed in commercial transmission electron microscopes. Low-energy electron diffraction and low-energy electron holography principles and experimental schemes are presented and discussed.
summary: This work details the advantages of using ultra-low energy electrons (20–300 eV) for imaging and diffraction, highlighting their high sensitivity and low radiation damage compared to conventional TEM. It presents theoretical and experimental methods, such as Low-Energy Electron Holography, for mapping both the amplitude and phase information of biological and material structures.
main_problem: The paper addresses the unique physical properties and applications of ultra-low energy electrons (20–300 eV) for high-sensitivity imaging and diffraction, contrasting them with conventional high-energy electron microscopy.
main_result: Low-energy electrons are superior for probing surfaces and biological samples due to low radiation damage, high sensitivity to local potentials, and the ability to perform phase-sensitive measurements via holography.
method: The discussion covers theoretical calculations of scattering amplitudes and differential cross-sections, alongside experimental techniques like Low-Energy Electron Diffraction (LEED) and Low-Energy Electron Holography (LEEH).
model_or_system: The physical system involves ultra-low energy electrons interacting with matter, such as graphene, DNA, and proteins. The analysis utilizes quantum mechanical principles to model electron scattering and wave propagation.
key_observables: Contrast in amplitude and phase distributions, cross-correlation coefficient for radiation damage, and the complex-valued exit wave.
important_parameters: Electron energy range (20–300 eV), wavelength ($\lambda \approx 1$ Å at 150 eV), and the Inelastic Mean Free Path (IMFP) which is minimized around 100 eV.
main_assumptions: The reconstruction of object properties from holograms and diffraction patterns is complicated by the strong phase shift acquired by low-energy electrons.
figures_summary: Figures compare Point Spread Functions (PSF) and Differential Cross-Sections (DCS) for different energies, show simulated complex exit waves through proteins, and demonstrate non-destructive imaging of DNA over extended periods.
paper_structure: The lecture progresses by detailing the unique properties of low-energy electrons (wavelength, scattering, damage), presenting the theoretical framework (calculations), and then discussing the application in specific techniques like LEED and LEEH.
why_interesting: The strong phase shift and the need for phase retrieval in LEEH provide a rich problem space connecting quantum wave mechanics to advanced experimental diagnostics, relevant to open quantum systems characterization.
